question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The player's remarkable consistent (a)/ performance in the series (b)/ won him the award. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• An adjective describes a noun, while an adverb describes an adjective, a verb or another adverb. "Consistent" is an adjective describing "performance", so the word that describes "consistent" must be an adverb. Hence "remarkable" must be "remarkably".

◦ Corrected sentence: The player's remarkably consistent performance in the series won him the award.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "performance in the series" is a proper noun phrase with a correct prepositional phrase.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "won him the award." is a proper simple past verb phrase, with "him" as the indirect object and "the award" as the direct object.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "remarkable" in part (a) is wrongly used in place of an adverb.

 

NOTE

 

• adverb + adjective + noun: remarkably consistent performance, unusually cold weather, deeply moving speech, highly qualified candidate — never remarkable consistent, unusual cold.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Not until the last guest had left, (a)/ the hostess could finally relax (b)/ and enjoy (c)/ a quiet cup of tea. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• When a sentence begins with "Not until + clause", the main clause takes inversion: the auxiliary comes before the subject. So "the hostess could finally relax" must be "did the hostess finally relax".

◦ Corrected sentence: Not until the last guest had left did the hostess finally relax and enjoy a quiet cup of tea.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Not until the last guest had left," is a proper opening clause, with the past perfect showing the earlier action and normal word order inside the "until" clause.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "and enjoy" is proper, because it is a parallel base form joined to "relax".

 

• Part (d) is correct — "a quiet cup of tea." is a proper object noun phrase, with "a" used before a consonant sound.

 

NOTE

 

• Not until + clause + auxiliary + subject + verb: Not until he apologised did she speak to him; the inversion is in the main clause, not in the "until" clause. Similar triggers: Only after, Only when, Never, Seldom, Hardly.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Speaking at the rally, (a)/ the minister said that (b)/ the government had launched recently a new scheme (c)/ to help small farmers. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• An adverb of time (recently, yesterday, today) is not placed between a verb and its object. It must come before the main verb or after the object. So "had launched recently a new scheme" must be "had recently launched a new scheme".

◦ Corrected sentence: Speaking at the rally, the minister said that the government had recently launched a new scheme to help small farmers.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Speaking at the rally," is a proper participial phrase, and its doer is the subject "the minister".

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the minister said that" is a proper reporting clause with "that".

 

• Part (d) is correct — "to help small farmers." is a proper infinitive phrase of purpose.

 

NOTE

 

• He completed the work quickly or He quickly completed the work, but never He completed quickly the work — adverbs of time, place and manner do not separate a verb from its direct object.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

This is the village (a)/ where my grandfather (b)/ was born and (c)/ lived in all his life. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Where" is a relative adverb and already means "in which", so the preposition "in" must not be repeated at the end of the clause. So "lived in all his life" must be "lived all his life".

◦ Corrected sentence: This is the village where my grandfather was born and lived all his life.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "This is the village" is a proper singular main clause.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "where my grandfather" is a proper relative clause, with "where" correctly used for a place.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "was born and" is a proper past form, with "was born" correctly used to give the birth.

 

NOTE

 

• relative adverbs: where = in / at which, when = on / at which, why = for which — the house where he lives (not the house where he lives in); the house in which he lives or the house he lives in.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The new recruit has (a)/ hardly no experience (b)/ of handling such cases. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Hardly" is already negative in meaning (= almost not), so it cannot be followed by another negative word such as "no". A double negative is wrong, so "hardly no experience" must be "hardly any experience".

◦ Corrected sentence: The new recruit has hardly any experience of handling such cases.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The new recruit has" is a proper singular subject with the singular verb "has".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "of handling such cases." is a proper gerund phrase, with the correct preposition "of" after "experience".

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because the double negative in part (b) is a mistake.

 

NOTE

 

• hardly / scarcely / barely + any / ever / anybody (not no / never / nobody): hardly any money, scarcely anybody, barely ever.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The milk left (a)/ outside the fridge (b)/ turned sourly (c)/ within a few hours. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Turn, become, grow, go, get, remain, seem, look, feel, taste, smell and sound are linking verbs when they show a state or a change of state, and a linking verb takes an adjective and not an adverb. Here "turned" means "became", so "sourly" must be "sour".

◦ Corrected sentence: The milk left outside the fridge turned sour within a few hours.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The milk left" is a proper subject, since "left" is a past participle that describes the milk.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "outside the fridge" is a proper prepositional phrase of place.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "within a few hours." is a proper prepositional phrase of time.

 

NOTE

 

• linking verb + adjective: The milk turned sour, He looked angry, The soup tastes good; action verb + adverb: She turned the key slowly, He looked at me angrily.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The pilot flew (a)/ low over the valley (b)/ and landed smoothly. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is grammatically correct. "Low" is a flat adverb (it has the same form as the adjective) and it correctly describes "flew". The form "lowly" is an adjective meaning humble, and it is not the adverb of "low" in this sense. "Smoothly" correctly describes "landed".

◦ Sentence as given: The pilot flew low over the valley and landed smoothly.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The pilot flew" is a proper singular subject with a simple past verb.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "low over the valley" is proper, with the flat adverb "low" and a correct prepositional phrase of place.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "and landed smoothly." is a proper compound verb in the simple past, with the adverb of manner "smoothly".

 

NOTE

 

• Do not over-correct flat adverbs: fly low, aim high, go straight, work hard, run fast, arrive early — they do not take "-ly" when the plain form is meant.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The scientist has decided (a)/ to pursue further research (b)/ by going to abroad. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Abroad" is an adverb of place meaning "in or to a foreign country", so it is not used with the preposition "to". So "going to abroad" must be "going abroad".

◦ Corrected sentence: The scientist has decided to pursue further research by going abroad.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The scientist has decided" is a proper singular subject with a present perfect verb.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "to pursue further research" is a proper infinitive phrase, with "research" used as an uncountable noun.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "to abroad" in part (c) is wrong.

 

NOTE

 

• go abroad, go home, come here, go there, go upstairs, go overseas (adverbs of place take no "to"); but go to the market, go to school (nouns take "to").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The seminar was (a)/ most over (b)/ when we reached (c)/ the auditorium. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The adverb that means "nearly" is "almost". "Most" means the greatest number or amount (most of the people, the most beautiful), so "most over" is wrong and must be "almost over".

◦ Corrected sentence: The seminar was almost over when we reached the auditorium.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The seminar was" is a proper singular subject with the singular verb "was".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "when we reached" is proper, because "reach" is a transitive verb and takes no preposition.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "the auditorium." is a proper object with the definite article.

 

NOTE

 

• almost (= nearly) — almost over, almost everyone; most (= the majority / superlative) — most of the people, the most beautiful; mostly (= mainly) — mostly farmers.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The boy very loves (a)/ his grandmother (b)/ and obeys (c)/ her every command. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Very" modifies adjectives and adverbs, but it cannot modify a verb. To strengthen a verb we use "very much" or "greatly". So "very loves" must be "very much loves".

◦ Corrected sentence: The boy very much loves his grandmother and obeys her every command.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "his grandmother" is a proper object noun phrase, with the possessive "his" agreeing with the male subject.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "and obeys" is a proper compound verb, with "obeys" agreeing with the singular subject "boy".

 

• Part (d) is correct — "her every command." is a proper object phrase, since "obey" takes its object directly.

 

NOTE

 

• very + adjective / adverb (very tall, very slowly); very much / greatly + verb (very much appreciate, greatly admire); much + comparative (much better).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Of all the candidates (a)/ who appeared for the interview, (b)/ Priya answered the questions (c)/ more confidently. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The comparative degree compares two persons or things, whereas the superlative degree is used for three or more. "Of all the candidates" refers to a whole group, so "more confidently" must be "most confidently".

◦ Corrected sentence: Of all the candidates who appeared for the interview, Priya answered the questions most confidently.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Of all the candidates" is a proper phrase, with "of all" followed by a plural noun.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "who appeared for the interview," is a proper relative clause, with the correct preposition "for" after "appeared".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "Priya answered the questions" is a proper subject and verb with an object, since "answer" is transitive and takes no preposition.

 

NOTE

 

• comparative (two) — more confidently than his brother; superlative (three or more) — most confidently of all, the best of all; adverbs of two or more syllables take more / most.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The tourist asked the guide (a)/ if there was a bus service (b)/ and how far was the temple (c)/ from the railway station. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In an indirect (reported) question introduced by how, when, where or why, the word order is that of a statement (subject + verb), and not that of a question. So "how far was the temple" must be "how far the temple was".

◦ Corrected sentence: The tourist asked the guide if there was a bus service and how far the temple was from the railway station.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The tourist asked the guide" is proper, since "ask" takes the person as its object.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "if there was a bus service" is a proper indirect yes/no question, with statement order.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "from the railway station." is a proper prepositional phrase of place.

 

NOTE

 

• direct — How far is the temple?; indirect — He asked how far the temple was; I wonder when he will come (not when will he come).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The more carefully he read the contract, (a)/ more discrepancies he found (b)/ in the clauses (c)/ that dealt with payment. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the pattern "The + comparative … the + comparative", both clauses begin with "the". The second clause here lacks it, so "more discrepancies he found" must be "the more discrepancies he found".

◦ Corrected sentence: The more carefully he read the contract, the more discrepancies he found in the clauses that dealt with payment.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The more carefully he read the contract," is a proper first half, with "the" and the comparative adverb "more carefully".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "in the clauses" is a proper prepositional phrase of place.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "that dealt with payment." is a proper relative clause, with "dealt with" as the correct phrasal verb.

 

NOTE

 

• The + comparative + subject + verb, the + comparative + subject + verb: The earlier you start, the sooner you finish; The higher the price, the lower the demand.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Rahul is late always (a)/ for the morning assembly, (b)/ and the teacher (c)/ has warned him repeatedly. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A frequency adverb (always, never, often, usually) is placed after the verb "be" (is / am / are / was / were). So "is late always" must be "is always late".

◦ Corrected sentence: Rahul is always late for the morning assembly, and the teacher has warned him repeatedly.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "for the morning assembly," is a proper prepositional phrase.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "and the teacher" is a proper singular subject.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "has warned him repeatedly." is a proper present perfect verb phrase, with the adverb "repeatedly" correctly placed at the end.

 

NOTE

 

• He is always late (after "be"); She always comes early (before a main verb); They have never met (after the first auxiliary).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

She threw the windows ___ open to let in the fresh morning air.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. wide.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Wide" is a flat adverb used with open, awake and apart (wide open, wide awake, wide apart) in the sense of "fully". "Widely" means "over a large area or by many people" (widely known), so the correct word here is "wide".

◦ Complete sentence: She threw the windows wide open to let in the fresh morning air.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "widely" — this means "by many people" or "over a large area", and it is not used with "open" in the sense of "fully".

 

• Option 2: "wider" — this is a comparative form, and no comparison is made in the sentence.

 

• Option 3: "widest" — this is a superlative form, and no comparison is made in the sentence.

 

NOTE

 

• wide (fully) — wide open, wide awake, wide apart; widely (by many people / over a large area) — widely known, widely used, widely travelled.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

No sooner had the bell rung when the students rushed out of the classroom.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. than.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "No sooner" is always followed by "than", never by "when". The full pattern is "No sooner + had + subject + V3 … than + simple past". So "when" must be "than".

◦ Corrected sentence: No sooner had the bell rung than the students rushed out of the classroom.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "then" — this is an adverb meaning "at that time", and it cannot join two clauses.

 

• Option 3: "that" — this is a conjunction used after "so" or "such", and not after "no sooner".

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "no sooner" cannot be followed by "when".

 

NOTE

 

• No sooner … than (No sooner had he arrived than it began to rain); Hardly / Scarcely / Barely … when (Hardly had he arrived when it began to rain).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The question paper was ___ lengthy that no student could complete it in the given time.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. so.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The pattern is "so + adjective + that" (cause and result). "Too" is followed by "to + verb", "such" is followed by "(a / an) + noun", and "very" does not take a "that" clause. So the correct word is "so".

◦ Complete sentence: The question paper was so lengthy that no student could complete it in the given time.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "too" — "too" goes with "to + verb" ("too lengthy to complete"), and it does not take a "that" clause.

 

• Option 2: "such" — "such" goes with a noun ("such a lengthy paper"), and not directly with an adjective.

 

• Option 3: "very" — "very" does not form a result clause with "that".

 

NOTE

 

• so + adjective / adverb + that (so tired that he slept); such + a + adjective + noun + that (such a tiring day that); too + adjective + to + verb (too tired to walk).

question: Select the sentence in which the adverb is used correctly.
option_1: Ravi did not pass the test, and so did Kiran.
option_2: Ravi passed the test, and so did Kiran.
option_3: Ravi passed the test, and neither did Kiran.
option_4: Ravi did not pass the test, and neither Kiran did.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Ravi passed the test, and so did Kiran.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Only Option 2 is correct. "So + auxiliary + subject" adds a similar positive statement, while "neither / nor + auxiliary + subject" adds a similar negative statement. The first clause in Option 2 is positive, so "so did Kiran" is correct.

◦ Correct sentence: Ravi passed the test, and so did Kiran.

 

• Each of the other three options contains a different error, explained below.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "Ravi did not pass the test, and so did Kiran." — the first clause is negative, so it needs "neither did Kiran" and not "so did Kiran".

 

• Option 3: "Ravi passed the test, and neither did Kiran." — the first clause is positive, so it needs "so did Kiran"; "neither" wrongly adds a negative idea.

 

• Option 4: "Ravi did not pass the test, and neither Kiran did." — "neither" is right, but the auxiliary must come before the subject: "neither did Kiran".

 

NOTE

 

• so + auxiliary + subject (positive) — so did she; neither / nor + auxiliary + subject (negative) — neither did she; the auxiliary must match the tense and the verb of the first clause.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The team had practised rigorously for months; ___, it lost the final match.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. however.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A conjunctive adverb joins two independent clauses and shows the relation between them. The second clause shows a contrast (practised hard, yet lost), so "however" is correct.

◦ Complete sentence: The team had practised rigorously for months; however, it lost the final match.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "moreover" — this adds a further point in the same direction, and it does not show a contrast.

 

• Option 3: "therefore" — this shows a result of the previous clause, and losing is not the result of practising hard.

 

• Option 4: "similarly" — this shows likeness or comparison, which does not fit here.

 

NOTE

 

• however / nevertheless (contrast); therefore / thus / hence (result); moreover / furthermore / besides (addition); a conjunctive adverb takes a semicolon before and a comma after it (…; however, it lost).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The tortoise cannot run as faster as the hare.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. fast.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the pattern "as + adjective / adverb + as", the positive degree is used and not the comparative. So "faster" must be "fast", and "fast" is a flat adverb that has the same form as the adjective.

◦ Corrected sentence: The tortoise cannot run as fast as the hare.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "fastly" — this is not a valid word, because "fast" is both an adjective and an adverb and takes no "-ly".

 

• Option 2: "fastest" — this is a superlative form, and "as … as" needs the positive degree.

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because the comparative "faster" cannot be used between "as … as".

 

NOTE

 

• as + positive + as (as fast as, as carefully as); comparative + than (faster than); never as faster as.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

We searched the whole house, but the missing documents were ___ to be found.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. nowhere.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Nowhere to be found" is the idiom that means "not to be found in any place". The word "but" also shows that the search failed, so "nowhere" is correct.

◦ Complete sentence: We searched the whole house, but the missing documents were nowhere to be found.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "anywhere" — this is used in negative or interrogative sentences ("not anywhere"), and it cannot give a negative sense in a positive sentence like this.

 

• Option 2: "somewhere" — this means "in some place", which suggests that the documents can be found and does not fit "but".

 

• Option 3: "everywhere" — this means "in all places", which contradicts the failed search shown by "but".

 

NOTE

 

• nowhere (in no place) — nowhere to be found; anywhere (negative / question) — I can't find it anywhere; somewhere (some unknown place); everywhere (in all places).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

No matter how hard did she try, she could not lift the heavy box.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. she tried.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After "no matter how / however / whatever" the clause keeps the normal order of a statement (subject + verb). There is no inversion and no auxiliary "did". The main clause "could not lift" is past, so the verb is "tried".

◦ Corrected sentence: No matter how hard she tried, she could not lift the heavy box.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "tried she" — the subject and verb are inverted, which is wrong after "no matter how".

 

• Option 2: "she tries" — the word order is right, but the present tense does not match the past "could not lift".

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because the question order "did she try" is wrongly used in a subordinate clause.

 

NOTE

 

• no matter how + adjective / adverb + subject + verb: No matter how fast he ran, However carefully she drove (no inversion); compare the inversion after negative adverbs: Never did he lie.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The committee has not announced the final list of candidates ___, although the deadline ended last week.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. yet.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In a negative sentence with the present perfect, "yet" used at the end means "up to now". "Still" goes before the verb, "already" is used in affirmative sentences, and "ever" does not give the sense of "up to now".

◦ Complete sentence: The committee has not announced the final list of candidates yet, although the deadline ended last week.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "still" — "still" is placed before the verb ("has still not announced"), and it is not used at the end of a negative sentence like this.

 

• Option 3: "already" — this is used in affirmative sentences, and it does not fit a negative statement.

 

• Option 4: "ever" — this means "at any time" and does not give the required sense of "up to now".

 

NOTE

 

• yet (negative / question, usually at the end) — He has not come yet, Has he come yet?; already (affirmative) — He has already come; still (continuing) — He is still waiting.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The Director has left the office ten minutes ago.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. left.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Ago" counts back from the present to a definite time in the past, so it is used with the simple past and not with the present perfect. So "has left" must be "left".

◦ Corrected sentence: The Director left the office ten minutes ago.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "is leaving" — the present continuous shows an action in progress, and it cannot go with a finished time such as "ten minutes ago".

 

• Option 3: "leaves" — the simple present cannot be used with "ago".

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "ago" cannot be used with the present perfect "has left".

 

NOTE

 

• ago + simple past (He left ten minutes ago); present perfect + just / already / yet / since / for (He has just left, He has left already).

question: Select the sentence that is grammatically incorrect.
option_1: Seldom does he miss a chance to help others.
option_2: Only by working hard can you achieve your goals.
option_3: Nowhere in the city can you find such peace.
option_4: Never before he had seen such a huge crowd.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Never before he had seen such a huge crowd.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Only Option 4 is incorrect. When a sentence begins with a negative or restrictive adverbial (never before, seldom, nowhere, only by …), the auxiliary comes before the subject (inversion). So "he had" must be "had he".

◦ Corrected sentence: Never before had he seen such a huge crowd.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is correct — "Seldom" is followed by the inverted "does he", with the base form "miss".

 

• Option 2 is correct — "Only by working hard" is followed by the inverted "can you".

 

• Option 3 is correct — "Nowhere in the city" is followed by the inverted "can you".

 

NOTE

 

• Seldom does he come, Only then did she speak, Nowhere can you find it, Never before had he seen it — the auxiliary comes before the subject after never, seldom, rarely, hardly, nowhere, only + adverbial.
